name: Case report / case series
short: Describe one or a few striking cases in detail. It raises a signal but can't test it.
gist: A detailed account of one or a few unusual cases. Raises a signal or a hypothesis; can't test it.
example: MMWR, June 1981: Pneumocystis pneumonia in five young men in Los Angeles, the first published description of AIDS.

ref.cite: Riley et al. (2017). CARE guidelines for case reports: explanation and elaboration document. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology.

name: Cross-sectional survey
short: One snapshot of a sample: how common things are, right now.
gist: Measure exposure and outcome in a sample at one moment. Estimates prevalence; can't show which came first.
example: National health interview surveys estimating smoking prevalence by age and region.

ref.cite: Wang & Cheng (2020). Cross-Sectional Studies. Chest.

name: Ecological study
short: Compare whole groups (countries, regions, years) using their averages.
gist: Compare groups (countries, regions, years) using aggregate data. A cheap hypothesis generator; individual-level conclusions are a trap.
example: Messerli (2012): national chocolate consumption vs. Nobel laureates per capita.

ref.cite: Morgenstern (1995). Ecologic Studies in Epidemiology: Concepts, Principles, and Methods. Annual Review of Public Health.

name: Monitoring / surveillance
short: Measure the same thing the same way, again and again, to catch trends.
gist: Systematic, repeated measurement of the same quantity across time and place to detect trends and signals.
example: The Mauna Loa CO₂ record (since 1958); post-marketing drug-safety pharmacovigilance.

ref.cite: Thacker & Berkelman (1988). Public health surveillance in the United States. Epidemiologic Reviews.

name: Capture–recapture
short: Sample twice and count the overlap: the fewer you recatch, the more there must be.
gist: Estimate the size of a population you can't count completely from the overlap between two or more independent samples or lists.
example: Petersen tagged plaice in the 1890s; epidemiologists now match overlapping disease registers the same way.

ref.cite: International Working Group for Disease Monitoring and Forecasting (1995). Capture-Recapture and Multiple-Record Systems Estimation I: History and Theoretical Development. American Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Prospective cohort
short: Measure exposure first, then follow people forward to see who gets the outcome.
gist: Measure exposures in people before outcomes happen, then follow them forward. Shows temporal order and incidence.
example: The Framingham Heart Study (1948–), which gave us the very idea of 'risk factors'.

ref.cite: Dawber et al. (1951). Epidemiological Approaches to Heart Disease: The Framingham Study. American Journal of Public Health and the Nations Health.

name: Retrospective cohort
short: Rebuild a cohort from old records and trace what happened to it.
gist: Reconstruct a cohort and its outcomes from existing records. Fast and cheap, but limited to what someone happened to record.
example: Occupational cohorts assembled from employment records, e.g. asbestos and shipyard workers.

ref.cite: Euser et al. (2009). Cohort Studies: Prospective versus Retrospective. Nephron Clinical Practice.

name: Case–control study
short: Start from the cases, find comparable controls, look back at exposures.
gist: Start from people with the outcome (cases) and comparable people without it (controls); compare their past exposures.
example: Doll & Hill (1950): smoking histories of lung-cancer patients vs. other hospital patients.

ref.cite: Doll & Hill (1950). Smoking and Carcinoma of the Lung. BMJ.

name: Case-crossover
short: Each case is their own control: what happened just before the event?
gist: Each case is their own control: compare exposure just before the event with the same person's exposure at other times.
example: Mittleman et al. (1993): heavy exertion as a trigger of heart attack within the hour.

ref.cite: Maclure (1991). The Case-Crossover Design: A Method for Studying Transient Effects on the Risk of Acute Events. American Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Target trial emulation
short: Design the ideal trial on paper, then emulate it in real-world data.
gist: Write the protocol of the trial you wish you could run, then emulate it step by step in observational data.
example: Hernán & Robins' framework; emulated trials of statins and vaccines using health records.

ref.cite: Hernán & Robins (2016). Using Big Data to Emulate a Target Trial When a Randomized Trial Is Not Available: Table 1. American Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Instrumental variable analysis
short: Use a natural nudge that changes the exposure, and nothing else.
gist: Find a factor that nudges the exposure but affects the outcome only through it: a natural coin flip.
example: Angrist & Krueger (1991): quarter of birth, compulsory schooling and earnings.

ref.cite: Angrist et al. (1996). Identification of Causal Effects Using Instrumental Variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association.

name: Mendelian randomization
short: Genes are shuffled at conception, which makes them nature's randomized trial.
gist: Use genetic variants as instruments. Genes are shuffled at conception, so carriers mimic a lifelong randomized trial.
example: LDL-lowering gene variants and coronary heart disease across large genetic consortia.

ref.cite: Davey Smith & Ebrahim (2003). ‘Mendelian randomization’: can genetic epidemiology contribute to understanding environmental determinants of disease?*. International Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Genome-wide association study
short: Test millions of genetic variants, one by one, for a link with a trait.
gist: Genotype many thousands of people and test each of millions of variants for association with a trait, with a very strict significance threshold.
example: WTCCC (2007): 2,000 cases each of seven common diseases against 3,000 shared controls.

ref.cite: Visscher et al. (2017). 10 Years of GWAS Discovery: Biology, Function, and Translation. The American Journal of Human Genetics.

name: Case-cohort / nested case–control
short: Measure the costly exposure only in the cases and a sample of the rest.
gist: Inside a cohort with stored samples, measure an expensive exposure only in all cases plus a random subcohort (or matched controls).
example: EPIC-InterAct: a random subcohort of about 16,000 drawn from 340,000 Europeans to study type 2 diabetes.

ref.cite: Prentice (1986). A case-cohort design for epidemiologic cohort studies and disease prevention trials. Biometrika.

name: Difference-in-differences
short: Compare the before–after change in a treated group with an untreated one.
gist: Compare the change over time in a group that got an intervention with the change in a similar group that didn't.
example: Card & Krueger (1994): New Jersey's minimum-wage rise vs. neighbouring Pennsylvania.

ref.cite: Wing et al. (2018). Designing Difference in Difference Studies: Best Practices for Public Health Policy Research. Annual Review of Public Health.

name: Regression discontinuity
short: A cutoff decides treatment: compare those just above with those just below.
gist: When a rule assigns treatment at a cutoff, compare units just above and just below: nearly identical except for treatment.
example: Angrist & Lavy (1999): Maimonides' rule capping class size at 40 pupils.

ref.cite: Thistlethwaite & Campbell (1960). Regression-discontinuity analysis: An alternative to the ex post facto experiment. Journal of Educational Psychology.

name: Interrupted time series
short: Many data points before and after a dated change: did the trend break?
gist: Many measurements before and after a dated intervention; test for a change in level or slope beyond the existing trend.
example: Hospital admissions for heart attacks before and after a public smoking ban.

ref.cite: Lopez Bernal et al. (2016). Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial. International Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Synthetic control
short: Build a weighted twin of one treated unit from untreated ones.
gist: Build a weighted 'twin' of one treated unit from untreated units that tracked it before the intervention; compare after.
example: Abadie et al.: California's 1988 tobacco programme; the economic cost of German reunification.

ref.cite: Abadie et al. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California’s Tobacco Control Program. Journal of the American Statistical Association.

name: Randomized controlled trial
short: Chance decides who gets the intervention. Then compare outcomes.
gist: Randomly allocate individuals to intervention or control, follow them up, compare outcomes. The benchmark for 'does it work?'
example: MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis (1948), the first modern randomized trial.

ref.cite: Medical Research Council (1948). Streptomycin Treatment of Pulmonary Tuberculosis: A Medical Research Council Investigation. BMJ.

name: Cluster randomized trial
short: Randomize whole groups (schools, villages, clinics), not individuals.
gist: Randomize whole groups (schools, clinics, villages) when the intervention acts at group level or would spill over.
example: School-based deworming and hygiene trials randomized by school.

ref.cite: Campbell et al. (2012). Consort 2010 statement: extension to cluster randomised trials. BMJ.

name: Crossover trial
short: Everyone gets both treatments, in random order, with a washout between.
gist: Each participant gets both treatments in random order, separated by a washout. Needs far fewer people.
example: Bioequivalence studies of generic versus brand-name drugs.

ref.cite: Mills et al. (2009). Design, analysis, and presentation of crossover trials. Trials.

name: Factorial experiment (DoE)
short: Vary several factors at once to find their effects and interactions.
gist: Vary several factors at once in a controlled setting. Estimates each effect and their interactions in few runs.
example: Fisher's agricultural experiments at Rothamsted; screening designs in process engineering.

ref.cite: Collins et al. (2009). Design of experiments with multiple independent variables: A resource management perspective on complete and reduced factorial designs. Psychological Methods.

name: N-of-1 trial
short: A randomized trial inside a single person.
gist: Repeated, randomized, ideally blinded treatment periods within a single patient to find out what works for them.
example: Personalized trials of pain or ADHD medication in individual patients.

ref.cite: Guyatt et al. (1986). Determining Optimal Therapy — Randomized Trials in Individual Patients. New England Journal of Medicine.

name: Stepped-wedge trial
short: Everyone gets it in the end; chance decides who goes first.
gist: All clusters start as controls and switch to the intervention at randomly ordered times until everyone has it.
example: The Gambia Hepatitis Intervention Study (1986), which phased in infant vaccination region by region.

ref.cite: Hussey & Hughes (2007). Design and analysis of stepped wedge cluster randomized trials. Contemporary Clinical Trials.

name: Online A/B test
short: Randomize users to two versions and watch what they do.
gist: Randomize users of a digital product to variants. Huge samples detect tiny effects within days.
example: Search and e-commerce platforms running thousands of controlled experiments a year.

ref.cite: Kohavi et al. (2007). Practical guide to controlled experiments on the web. Proceedings of the 13th ACM SIGKDD international conference on Knowledge discovery and data mining.

name: Adaptive / platform trial
short: One master trial: arms are dropped and added as evidence arrives.
gist: One master protocol tests many treatments against a shared control; arms are dropped or added as data accrue.
example: RECOVERY (COVID-19): dexamethasone shown to save lives within about 100 days of launch.

ref.cite: Woodcock & LaVange (2017). Master Protocols to Study Multiple Therapies, Multiple Diseases, or Both. New England Journal of Medicine.

name: Field experiment
short: Randomize and manipulate in the real world: plots, islands, markets.
gist: Manipulate a factor in the real world (plots, islands, villages, markets) with randomized replicates and controls.
example: Paine (1966, 1969): removing Pisaster starfish from a rocky shore collapsed its diversity: the 'keystone species'.

ref.cite: Paine (1966). Food Web Complexity and Species Diversity. The American Naturalist.

name: Ethnography
short: Live inside the setting for months and learn how it really works.
gist: Immerse yourself in a setting for months, observing and taking part, to understand practices and meanings from the inside.
example: Whyte's Street Corner Society (1943); Latour & Woolgar's Laboratory Life (1979).

ref.cite: Reeves et al. (2008). Qualitative research methodologies: ethnography. BMJ.

name: Grounded theory
short: Build a new theory, step by step, up from the data.
gist: Collect and analyse data in iterative cycles (coding, comparing, sampling) to build a new theory from the ground up.
example: Glaser & Strauss (1965), Awareness of Dying: how hospital staff and patients manage knowledge of death.

ref.cite: Glaser & Strauss (1967; 2017 edition). The discovery of grounded theory: strategies for qualitative research. Routledge.

name: Interviews & thematic analysis
short: Ask, listen, and find the patterns in what people say.
gist: In-depth interviews or focus groups analysed for patterns of meaning. Answers 'how' and 'why' from people's own view.
example: Exploring why patients stop taking a medication they were prescribed.

ref.cite: Braun & Clarke (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology.

name: Case study (in-depth)
short: One bounded case, examined from every angle in its real context.
gist: Study one or a few bounded cases (a company, a project, a policy) in their real context, using many sources of evidence.
example: Allison's Essence of Decision (1971) on the Cuban missile crisis; engineering failure investigations.

ref.cite: Crowe et al. (2011). The case study approach. BMC Medical Research Methodology.

name: Process tracing
short: Test rival causal stories inside one case, clue by clue.
gist: Test rival explanations of one case against the evidence each predicts, step by step: hoop tests can rule one out, smoking guns confirm one.
example: Van Evera's (1997) hoop and smoking-gun tests, now a standard tool in political science.

ref.cite: Collier (2011). Understanding Process Tracing. PS: Political Science & Politics.

name: Delphi consensus
short: Experts vote anonymously, round after round, until they converge.
gist: Experts rate statements anonymously over repeated rounds, seeing the group's feedback, until consensus emerges.
example: COMET-initiative 'core outcome sets' that tell trialists what every trial in a field should measure.

ref.cite: Dalkey & Helmer (1963). An Experimental Application of the DELPHI Method to the Use of Experts. Management Science.

name: Mixed methods (sequential)
short: Numbers then stories to explain them, or stories then numbers to test them.
gist: Combine numbers and narratives in sequence: a survey then interviews to explain it, or interviews then a survey to test them.
example: Explanatory sequential design: a survey finds a gap, follow-up interviews explain it.

ref.cite: Johnson & Onwuegbuzie (2004). Mixed Methods Research: A Research Paradigm Whose Time Has Come. Educational Researcher.

name: Systematic review & meta-analysis
short: Find every study on a focused question, appraise them, pool them.
gist: A pre-specified, exhaustive search and appraisal of all studies on a focused question; pool results where sensible.
example: Cochrane reviews; the antenatal-steroids forest plot in the Cochrane logo.

ref.cite: Page et al. (2021). The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ.

name: Scoping review
short: Map what has been studied on a broad topic, and where the gaps are.
gist: Systematically map what research exists on a broad topic (concepts, methods, gaps) without pooling effects.
example: PRISMA-ScR guided maps, e.g. of how AI is used in nursing practice.

ref.cite: Arksey & O'Malley (2005). Scoping studies: towards a methodological framework. International Journal of Social Research Methodology.

name: Network meta-analysis
short: Rank many treatments at once from direct and indirect comparisons.
gist: Compare many treatments at once by combining direct and indirect evidence across a network of trials.
example: Cipriani et al. (2018): 21 antidepressants ranked from 522 trials.

ref.cite: Lumley (2002). Network meta-analysis for indirect treatment comparisons. Statistics in Medicine.

name: Individual participant data meta-analysis
short: Pool every trial's raw data, not just its published summary.
gist: Collect and reanalyse each trial's individual participant data, so outcomes, subgroups and analyses are defined the same way everywhere.
example: The Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group, pooling patient-level data from adjuvant-therapy trials since 1985.

ref.cite: Riley et al. (2010). Meta-analysis of individual participant data: rationale, conduct, and reporting. BMJ.

name: Umbrella review
short: A review of reviews: the big picture across a whole field.
gist: A review of systematic reviews: summarizes and grades the evidence across many reviews on a broad topic.
example: Theodoratou et al. (2014): vitamin D and 137 outcomes across meta-analyses and trials.

ref.cite: Ioannidis (2009). Integration of evidence from multiple meta-analyses: a primer on umbrella reviews, treatment networks and multiple treatments meta-analyses. Canadian Medical Association Journal.

name: Rapid review
short: A systematic review on a deadline, with its shortcuts declared.
gist: A systematic review with transparently streamlined steps, delivered in weeks to inform an urgent decision.
example: Cochrane Rapid Reviews informing COVID-19 policy in 2020.

ref.cite: Tricco et al. (2015). A scoping review of rapid review methods. BMC Medicine.

name: Realist review
short: What works, for whom, in what context, and why?
gist: Synthesize mixed evidence to explain how complex programmes work: for whom, in what contexts, and why.
example: Pawson's realist syntheses of complex social programmes (context + mechanism → outcome).

ref.cite: Pawson et al. (2005). Realist review - a new method of systematic review designed for complex policy interventions. Journal of Health Services Research & Policy.

name: Prior art review
short: Before you build it or call it new, search patents, products and papers for what already exists.
gist: Search patents, standards, products, theses and papers for what already exists, before you build, publish or claim novelty.
example: In re Hall (1986): one German thesis, shelved in a university library, counted as prior art against a US patent.

ref.cite: 35 U.S.C. § 102: Conditions for patentability; novelty. United States Code.

name: Co-citation analysis
short: Two works are linked whenever a later paper cites both. Clusters reveal a field's foundations.
gist: Link works (or authors) each time later papers cite them together; clusters map a field's intellectual base. New papers are invisible.
example: Small (1973) defined it; White & Griffith (1981) mapped information science's schools by author co-citation.

ref.cite: Small (1973). Co-citation in the scientific literature: A new measure of the relationship between two documents. Journal of the American Society for Information Science.

name: Bibliographic coupling
short: Two papers are linked when they cite the same sources. Clusters reveal today's research fronts.
gist: Link papers that share references; clusters map current research fronts. Works the day a paper appears, but generic references blur it.
example: Kessler (1963) grouped physics papers by the references they share; still a standard way to find research fronts.

ref.cite: Kessler (1963). Bibliographic coupling between scientific papers. American Documentation.

name: Multivocal literature review
short: Review papers and practitioners' blogs, talks and white papers, grading each source.
gist: A systematic review that adds grey literature (blogs, white papers, talks) when practice outruns research, and grades each source.
example: Garousi, Felderer & Mäntylä (2019) set the guidelines, after an MLR on when to automate software tests.

ref.cite: Garousi, Felderer & Mäntylä (2019). Guidelines for including grey literature and conducting multivocal literature reviews in software engineering. Information and Software Technology.

name: Diagnostic accuracy study
short: The new test and the reference standard, on the same real patients.
gist: Apply a new test and a reference standard to consecutive people suspected of the condition; estimate sensitivity and specificity.
example: STARD-reported evaluations of rapid antigen tests against PCR.

ref.cite: Bossuyt et al. (2015). STARD 2015: an updated list of essential items for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies. BMJ.

name: Reliability & agreement study
short: Do raters, devices or repeated measurements agree?
gist: Repeat measurements across raters, occasions or devices; quantify agreement (kappa, ICC, Bland–Altman limits).
example: Bland & Altman (1986): why correlation is the wrong way to compare two measurement methods.

ref.cite: Bland & Altman (1986). Statistical methods for assessing agreement between two methods of clinical measurement. The Lancet.

name: Instrument development & validation
short: Build a questionnaire or scale, and prove it measures what it claims.
gist: Build a questionnaire or scale from theory and input, then test its structure, reliability and validity (psychometrics).
example: Development of the Maslach Burnout Inventory (1981).

ref.cite: Clark & Watson (1995). Constructing validity: Basic issues in objective scale development. Psychological Assessment.

name: Nomological network study
short: Predict how your measure should relate to other measures, then test the whole pattern.
gist: From theory, predict which measures yours should track, which it shouldn't, and which groups should differ; then test the whole pattern.
example: Cronbach & Meehl (1955) coined the idea; Campbell & Fiske's (1959) multitrait–multimethod matrix put it to work.

ref.cite: Cronbach & Meehl (1955). Construct validity in psychological tests. Psychological Bulletin.

name: Discrete choice experiment
short: Make people choose between bundles of features to reveal what they really value.
gist: Respondents choose between hypothetical options whose attributes vary by design; choice models reveal trade-offs and willingness to pay.
example: McFadden's random-utility models (Nobel prize, 2000), first used to forecast ridership of San Francisco's BART.

ref.cite: de Bekker-Grob, Ryan & Gerard (2010). Discrete choice experiments in health economics: a review of the literature. Health Economics.

name: Interlaboratory comparison
short: Same sample, many labs: how reproducible is the method?
gist: Identical samples go to many labs (a 'round robin'); differences reveal how reproducible a measurement method is.
example: Proficiency-testing schemes; BIPM key comparisons between national metrology institutes.

ref.cite: Thompson et al. (2006). The International Harmonized Protocol for the proficiency testing of analytical chemistry laboratories (IUPAC Technical Report). Pure and Applied Chemistry.

name: Analytical / mathematical theory
short: Derive it with mathematics: what must be true, in every case.
gist: Derive results from first principles with mathematics: proofs, closed-form solutions, bounds. 'What must be true if…'
example: Carnot's efficiency limit (1824); Nash equilibrium (1950).

ref.cite: May (2004). Uses and Abuses of Mathematics in Biology. Science.

name: Computational simulation
short: Build the system in a computer and run the experiments reality won't allow.
gist: Encode mechanisms in a model (FEM, CFD, Monte Carlo, agent-based) and run experiments impossible, dangerous or too costly in reality.
example: Numerical-relativity waveforms of black-hole mergers, computed years before LIGO's first detection.

ref.cite: Sargent (2013). Verification and validation of simulation models. Journal of Simulation.

name: Prediction model (statistical / ML)
short: Learn from past data to forecast who or what comes next.
gist: Develop a model that forecasts an outcome from predictors, then test its discrimination and calibration on new data.
example: The Framingham risk score; TRIPOD-reported clinical prediction models.

ref.cite: Collins et al. (2015). Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis (TRIPOD): the TRIPOD statement. BMJ.

name: Cost-effectiveness analysis
short: Weigh the extra cost against the extra benefit: is it worth the money?
gist: Compare the costs and outcomes of alternatives, often in a decision model, to find the extra cost per unit of benefit, such as per QALY gained.
example: NICE in England weighs new medicines by their cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained.

ref.cite: Sanders et al. (2016). Recommendations for Conduct, Methodological Practices, and Reporting of Cost-effectiveness Analyses. JAMA.

name: Design science (build & evaluate)
short: Build an artifact that solves a real problem, and test it with its users.
gist: Iteratively design an artifact (device, software, method) that solves a real problem, and evaluate it with users in context.
example: Usability-engineered medical devices (IEC 62366); research software built with its users.

ref.cite: Hevner et al. (2004). Design science in information systems research. MIS Quarterly.

name: Pilot / feasibility study
short: A dress rehearsal: can the big study actually be run?
gist: A small rehearsal of a future study. Can we recruit, retain, deliver and measure? Not for estimating effects.
example: CONSORT extension for randomized pilot and feasibility trials (2016).

ref.cite: Eldridge et al. (2016). CONSORT 2010 statement: extension to randomised pilot and feasibility trials. BMJ.

name: Usability test (think-aloud)
short: Watch real users try real tasks while they say what they're thinking.
gist: Representative users attempt realistic tasks with a prototype while thinking aloud; observers log where and why they struggle.
example: Nielsen & Landauer (1993): about five users find most usability problems in one round of testing.

ref.cite: Ericsson & Simon (1980). Verbal reports as data. Psychological Review.

name: Plan–Do–Study–Act cycles
short: Small, fast tests of change: try it, measure it, adapt it, repeat.
gist: Iterative small-scale tests of a change in a real service, each measured over time on a run chart and used to plan the next cycle.
example: The Institute for Healthcare Improvement's Model for Improvement, used in hospitals worldwide.

ref.cite: Taylor et al. (2013). Systematic review of the application of the plan–do–study–act method to improve quality in healthcare. BMJ Quality & Safety.

name: Benchmark evaluation
short: Same tasks, same data, same metrics: who really performs best?
gist: Compare methods on shared tasks, datasets and metrics under identical conditions, with baselines, ablations and repeated runs.
example: ImageNet; robot-grasping benchmarks built on the YCB object set.

ref.cite: Sim et al. (2003). Using benchmarking to advance research: a challenge to software engineering. 25th International Conference on Software Engineering, 2003. Proceedings..
